claims.text: The HEA was initially designed as a single-phase solid solution.
Under tensile loading representative of demanding service, the HEA loses toughness.
Discrete slip avalanches coalesce into localized shear bands under demanding tensile loading.
Localized shear bands act as precursors to brittle fracture.
The initial material has a homogeneous, defect-scarce microstructure.
Varying tensile strain rate and temperature provides a controlled way to reproduce different demanding service conditions.
Localized slip avalanches coalesce into shear bands that lead to microcrack initiation.
At high strain rates or increased stress, slip events cease to be uniformly distributed and cluster spatially.
Spatial clustering of slip events creates stress localization.
Stress localization can overcome the alloy's inherent toughness and initiate brittle fracture.
At lower loading rates, the baseline alloy exhibits ductile behavior.
High strain rate or elevated loading will increase slip-avalanche intensity relative to the baseline.
Increased slip-avalanche intensity will produce more localized deformation.
High strain rate or elevated loading will reduce elongation to failure and toughness relative to the baseline.
High strain rate or elevated loading will produce brittle-fracture evidence such as sudden crack propagation.
Under moderate strain-rate loading, the original material exhibits uniform plastic deformation and high toughness.
High load, rapid strain rate, or temperature variation can drive slip-avalanche dynamics beyond the stability limit for homogeneous plastic flow.
Submicroscopic phase changes may also influence fracture behavior.
The critical strain rate and stress magnitude for localization-induced brittle failure are not specified.
Failure to observe both increased localization and decreased ductility under demanding loading relative to baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
